Try incorporating the other senses (smell, taste, touch [breeze, texture, etc.], balance, hunger, unease, etc.) into your descriptions. The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy did a great job making the "Pan Galactic Gargle Baster" part of its world, and in doing so made the world that much more captivating.

Saying that the player sees dust motes in the air and a set of foot prints in the dust is good. Mentioning the musty odor of mildew, the resistance of the rusting hinges, the way the smoke from the torches clog clings to the ceiling and hangs unmoving will add additional layers of texture and life to your world.

Instead of simply hearing footsteps, do you hear the creaking of floor beams or the clicking of heels on stone?

Going a step forward when your party is in an inn/restaurant/cantina/space station what is the local flavor? Does the food have a metallic taste that is barely washed away by the bland and distilled water? When your party orders wine are they given a strong fortified wine, something sweet, or perhaps a spicy and flavorful mixture?

If we use this to describe portions of a city what is the smell? The immigrant enclave perhaps has a unique aroma with foreign spices, while the adventurer quarter has a familiar smell of fried fish, meat pies, and other bland comfort food.
